seasons.review_body: This Is Going to Hurt arrived in February 2022 with 96% on Rotten Tomatoes from 45 critics and a 91 Metascore - the rare adaptation that surpasses the source material in the opinion of most reviewers. Adam Kay's bestselling memoir becomes seven episodes of controlled fury: junior doctor Adam (Ben Whishaw) navigates obstetrics and gynaecology night shifts in 2006 while his personal life disintegrates under the pressure. The Atlantic called it more accurate and wrenching than any medical drama on television. Vanity Fair praised its "chilling glimpse of the real stakes in the reproductive rights conversation." BAFTA agreed emphatically - Whishaw won Best Actor, the show won Best Writer, Best Casting, and Best Editing. Ambika Mod's debut as registrar Shruti was singled out as a revelation. The finale generated significant conversation for its willingness to go to genuinely dark places.

episode_reviews.review_body:
# This Is Going To Hurt S1E1: "Episode 1" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

Someone tells **Adam** there has been an accident, and the hour never lets that sentence sit still. A baby is lying sideways. A Cesarean Section becomes necessary. A staff lift emergency reveals a cord prolapse, and the corridor becomes the route to theater. The premiere's thesis is already in motion: medicine here is action under pressure, then paperwork under pressure. The scalpel is urgent. The notes are dangerous. The episode works best when it treats competence as something that has to survive speed, blame, and the system waiting at the end of the shift.

## A Hospital That Introduces Itself in Crisis

The premiere does not warm up. It begins with a message, an accident, and a labor ward emergency that immediately narrows the world to movement. **Andrea** is told the baby is sideways and needs a Cesarean Section, then the staff lift situation is identified as a cord prolapse. That sequencing matters. The hour makes obstetrics feel less like a department than a chain reaction, where one phrase can change the room faster than any speech.

The early doctor-admission framing, capped by Welcome to the NHS, works because it is placed against this rush. The line is not treated as a brochure slogan. It lands like a dare. Here is the institution. Now run.

That is the premiere's cleanest craft decision: it teaches the workplace through emergency procedure. Cord prolapse, Cesarean Section, theater, escalation. The words are technical, but the drama is blunt. Someone has to know what is happening. Someone has to decide. Someone has to move the patient.

The danger is that the episode can feel front-loaded with incident, but the compression has a point. It makes Adam's job look impossible before it makes his choices look questionable. That order is crucial. If the show opened with blame, Adam would flatten into a cautionary tale. It opens with speed, so the later blame has teeth.

## Adam's Confidence Has a Clock On It

**Adam** wants to act. That is the clearest line through the hour. He wants to handle emergencies directly, follow through on operations, and trust his judgment when the situation is moving faster than the chain of command. The episode gives him an environment that rewards that instinct at first. A labor ward emergency cannot be committee-managed into safety. A cord prolapse does not wait for emotional clarity.

Then the hour tightens the trap. At 25 weeks, a Grade one Cesarean Section is called, anesthetics are requested, and Adam again becomes the figure through whom urgency is converted into action. The episode understands the appeal of that kind of doctor: quick, certain, useful. He can name the emergency and push the room toward theater.

That is only the first half of the argument.

The central turn arrives when Adam says the woman is going to die and it is his fault. The writing earns that moment because it has already shown why he would trust himself. His confidence does not come from swagger alone. It comes from a workplace where hesitation can be lethal. The same impulse that makes him valuable can also leave him exposed. The episode's strongest idea is that emergency medicine does not separate heroism and liability neatly. It lets them share a corridor.

## Tracy Carries the Risk the Rush Keeps Missing

**Tracy** is the hour's corrective pressure. She wants correct high-risk assessment and proper escalation, and the episode gives her a position that is less flashy than Adam's but structurally vital. She calls in Adam's help, which keeps her from becoming simple opposition. She understands that a crisis needs action. Later, she frames the situation as preventable if blood testing had been done, which gives the episode its essential counterweight.

That tension is productive. Tracy participates in the emergency response, then forces the aftermath to account for what preceded it. Escalation arrives late if the assessment before it is wrong.

This is where the premiere starts becoming more than a hectic hospital shift. The early movement toward theater gives the episode adrenaline. Tracy's position gives it moral shape. If the medical emergency is the visible fire, her concern is the wiring behind the wall. The character work lands because the episode lets procedural detail carry personality. Adam is defined by action under pressure. Tracy is defined by the question that follows action: why did the pressure become this bad?

The writing could have made that conflict louder. It is better because it keeps the dispute practical. Blood testing, escalation, preventability. No grand speech needed. The system speaks in omissions.

## The Hour Cuts Away When It Should Squeeze

The episode's weakness comes from the same ambition that gives it texture. The event density is high: accident, sideways baby, cord prolapse, theater, a 25-week Grade one Cesarean Section, then the admission of possible fault and a documentation dispute. Against that, the hour uses long, stylized insert dialogue and monologue moments, with transition silences that create pacing dips rather than sustained calm.

Some of that contrast works. A show built only from alarm bells would become noise. The pauses let the pressure register and give the premiere a more jagged rhythm than a straight procedural sprint. The problem is placement. When the medical chain is escalating, any stylized interruption has to cut sharper than the emergency around it. A few moments soften the grip instead.

That matters because this episode's best mode is acceleration with consequence. The labor ward material has forward pull. The later accountability beat has a hard snap. The dips between them do not break the hour, but they make the structure feel occasionally self-conscious. The premiere wants the rush of a bad shift and the shape of a confessional drama. It mostly holds those modes in line, but the strain shows during transitions.

Still, the issue is calibration. The hour knows what pressure does. It only occasionally lets style arrive one beat too early.

## The Amendment Is the Real Knife

The final accountability beat reframes the episode. **Adam's supervisor** orders an amendment: "Write that you discussed with me over the phone." That instruction is cold because it turns a medical crisis into a record-keeping crisis without lowering the stakes. The patient may be the immediate emergency, but the written account becomes the battlefield.

This is where the premiere's opening movement pays off. The early scenes build a case for urgency. The closing scene builds a case for consequence. Adam wanted to act on his own judgment, including around operations and patient management. By the end, he is forced into a version of events where the correct advice is tied to a phone discussion and sending the patient home. The issue expands from what happened to who will carry the official shape of what happened.

That is a sharper ending than another medical escalation would have been. The episode plants open loops with discipline: what outcome follows the amendment, whether Adam's decision-making will be addressed beyond that instruction, and how the cord prolapse chain resolves without further visible harm. The premiere leaves its biggest wound on the page, not in the operating theater. That is the craft.

## The Verdict

This Is Going To Hurt opens with a fierce, well-built hour that understands emergency medicine as a collision between speed and accountability. The labor ward material gives the premiere immediate charge, Adam's contradiction gives it a spine, and Tracy's insistence on assessment keeps the drama from turning into pure workplace chaos. The score is held back by pacing dips in the stylized inserts and transitions, which occasionally drain pressure from an episode designed around escalation. Still, the final amendment lands hard because the hour has earned the shift from action to liability. BollyAI's score: 8.0/10. As a season opener, it plants a strong accountability thread around documentation, judgment, and whether the system protects patients, doctors, or its own record.

Written by BollyAI, reviewed by our editorial team.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 7
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale generated the most critical discussion of any single episode in 2022 British television. It pays off every tonal promise made in the first episode - the comedy drops entirely, and what remains is one of the most serious statements British TV has made about the human cost of an underfunded health system.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The final sequence recontextualises the entire series in a way that demands a second viewing of every prior episode.
